title: U.S. Open disputes ‘The VIP List’ food influencers’ account of credentials being revoked
content:
The U.S. Open has disputed two prominent New York influencers’ account that they were kicked out of the tournament for posting images of their credentials online.

Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens run New York restaurant and lifestyle platform The VIP List. It has more than 440,000 followers on TikTok and 150,000 on Instagram. During an interview with TMZ, Radice and Jongens said that they received their credentials through a partnership with a restaurant at the tournament. They planned to produce content for that restaurant from the U.S. Open.

They said that they believed their access had been withdrawn around two hours after arriving at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center because they had posted images of their passes online, but a spokesperson for the USTA said that Radice and Jongens’ access was revoked because they had been improperly submitted as vendor staff.

“These individuals were not credentialed as media or content creators,” Brendan McIntyre, the USTA’s managing director and head of U.S. Open, professional tennis and USA Tennis content and communications, said in a statement sent to The Athletic. “They were improperly submitted for credentials on a staff list provided by a food vendor.”

Radice, Jongens and the food vendor that submitted them for credentials have been contacted for comment.

The 2026 U.S. Open terms governing media and content creator credentials do separately state that holders must not publish or distribute an image or video of their credential, including on social media.

The U.S. Open began credentialing content creators as media in 2025, when 54 were approved. Close to 100 were approved for this year’s tournament.

The incident comes in the background of a heightened focus on the presence — and impact — of content creators on the event following a number of incidents, most prominently inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, the biggest court at the tournament. During two-time champion Naomi Osaka’s opening match against Anastasia Zakharova, the chair umpire paused play because of an ad-hoc photoshoot going on in the stands.

Messages reading, “Please refrain from the use of flash photography or other lighting during match play. Thank you and enjoy the tennis!” have been flashed on jumbotrons at the biggest stadiums intermittently.

But Arthur Ashe Stadium being loud, filled with fans taking flash photos and sipping on Honey Deuce cocktails at $23 a piece is nothing new. While corporate sponsors and the USTA alike have recognized the benefit of broadening the scope of how they reach audiences — and potential clients and ticket buyers — the tournament has always flown in the face of traditional, oftentimes staid and buttoned-up tennis etiquette. This incident, according to the tournament, was not part of all that.

“We go every year, we are diehard tennis fans,” Radice and Jongens said.

“It is literally our dream. … We were there to be respectful and follow the rules.”
